entries.misconception: We can read the pictures instead of the words.
entries.identify: Ask learners to talk about a picture. Then together read the words on the page. Are they the same thing?
entries.overcome: Discuss the fact that although pictures can support our understanding and add extra information, we also have to read (decode and understand) the words on the page. For each topic, there is a selection of starter ideas, main teaching ideas and plenary ideas. You can pick out individual ideas and mix and match them depending on the needs of your class. The activities include suggestions for how they can be differentiated or used for assessment. Homework ideas are also provided.

entries.misconception: Story titles tell you what happens in a story.
entries.identify: Show learners a range of storybooks and discuss the titles. You may include Don’t Spill the Milk! Ask how many learners think titles are: • for telling you what happens in a story • for giving you an idea of what a story is about. • Nothing to do with the story.
entries.overcome: Create a class display of story titles the class have read and enjoyed. When learners are writing their own stories, remind them that a title should not tell us what happens and spoil the story.

entries.misconception: The letter a at the end of word always sounds like /a/ for apple.
entries.identify: Ask learners to tell you the name of the girl and teacher in the story Hide and Seek. Listen to their pronunciations of Zara and Miss Garcia. Can they hear that the final a should be unstressed, as in schwa? This sound is more like an ugh sound!
entries.overcome: Remind learners when they are reading aloud or spelling that sometimes they might need to try to use this ugh sound for letter a to help them to work out the word or its spelling, especially if the word ends in a.

entries.misconception: Listening well is only about using our ears.
entries.identify: Ask learners to listen to the opening of the rhyming story. Ask what they hear. (words, a voice) Ask them what the words and voice are telling them. (names, an adventure, that it’s nighttime, where they are going …)
entries.overcome: Talk about good listening strategies. Ask: What helps us to hear more than just words and a voice or music? Should we close our eyes? Listen several times? Talk with a partner to share ideas? Create a poster of ‘Good Listening Skills’ for the classroom.

entries.misconception: We can use the word thing to talk about people.
entries.identify: Ask learners: Can we say: Bear asked everything? (No, because we use thing to talk about ‘things’ and body or one to talk about people or animals. So here, we would say: Bear asked everybody.)
entries.overcome: Make a class poster or display to show these useful words and their relationship to each other. Anything/something/everything Anybody/somebody/everybody

entries.misconception: We only need a few words to describe things in detail.
entries.identify: Ask the class to listen to you describing something simple in the class. Ask them if you had to use a few or a lot of words to make your description.
entries.overcome: Show learners how using more words make it easier to understand what is being described. Begin with few words. e.g. it’s blue. Gradually build your description by adding words to show how more words makes the description clearer. Remind learners of this in their own speech and writing.

entries.misconception: We only use capital letters at the beginning of a sentence and to begin our names.
entries.identify: Ask learners to find examples in the story text (or cloze) of capital letters and to explain why they are used, e.g. at the beginning of sentences/questions; for emphasis or to show emotion: YOU! … Encourage learners to use this technique in their own writing.
entries.overcome: Practise the formation of capital letters so they feel confident to use these.

entries.misconception: Mistakes are bad.
entries.identify: Ask learners if they can remember a time when they made a mistake. Ask them how they felt. Did they learn from it? Have a sensitive class discussion about the value of mistakes.
entries.overcome: Establish a classroom culture where mistakes are welcomed as opportunities to learn.

entries.misconception: When there are two consonants next to each other, we always say two sounds.
entries.identify: Write the words shop, chat ticket and train on the board. Ask learners to sound out each letter sound (phoneme) and blend to read the words, e.g. ch-a-t; sh-o-p; t-i-ck- e-t; t-r-ai-n. Listen out for any learners who are saying two separate sounds for two consonants together. Ask: What is different about the last word? (We say a letter sound for each of the two consonants at the start of the word, instead of saying one sound for both.) Find different examples of words with digraphs, e.g. chick, fish, and/or adjacent consonants at the beginning and end of words, e.g. stop, jump.
entries.overcome: Use the Workbook Session 2.1 activities and the Phonics

entries.misconception: Information books only have photos.
entries.identify: Ask learners to look at a collection of non-fiction texts (mainly recounts if possible). Ask them to talk about the different types of illustration and photos.
entries.overcome: Discuss the fact that we can illustrate stories and non-fiction books in different ways to give different information. Share a recount text such as My First Train Trip to demonstrate an interesting mix of photos and illustrations combined.

entries.misconception: Letter X is code for letter sound /z/. Ask learners to say the word xylophone! (or any learner’s name in your class with a name beginning with X and sounded as /z/, e.g. Xanthe.

entries.overcome: Make a class display of X words – very few require the letter sound /z/ as in xylophone.

entries.misconception: We always say every letter in a word.
entries.identify: Write the word Wednesday on the board. Ask learners to say each letter sound, e.g. blend to read the word W-e-d-n-e-s-d-a-y Ask how you can split the word to make it easier. (W-e-d/n-e-s/d-a-y) When learners say Wed-nes-day, ask them if that sounds right. Say: We say: Wens-day.
entries.overcome: Establish that in some words there are letters that we do not need to pronounce. When they meet other silent letters in words during their reading, remind them of the Wednesday example.

entries.misconception: All question words begin with wh.
entries.identify: Ask learners to think about what question words begin with and list question words they know. Take ideas and keep going until how is mentioned.
entries.overcome: Talk about how most question words begin with wh but that how does not. Make a class list or poster of question words to use when learners need support.

entries.misconception: Long words are hard to read.
entries.identify: Write the word roundabout on the board. Ask learners to read it. Ask: Can anyone read this word? How? What did you do? They may have started blending then guessed, split it into two and blended each smaller word, etc. If no one can read the word, then model the technique of clapping the word and splitting it into two: round/about; r/ou/n/d round; a/b/ou/t about = roundabout.
entries.overcome: Remind learners, when they are reading aloud or spelling, that sometimes they can try to work out a longer word by splitting it into smaller parts. Provide practice by giving learners longer words to work out.

entries.misconception: It does not matter if we use he or she to talk about boys and girls or men and women.
entries.identify: Ask learners to say what is wrong in sentences you are reading aloud. For example: The boy loved the Slide and Glide. She loved to splash. Polly and Sal waited in the café because Dad was parking the car. She said to wait there. Polly was happy. He was going to have a lovely birthday.
entries.overcome: Talk about pronouns for males and females. Make a class display of pronouns that learners can use when they are unsure. Add pictures to help learners distinguish the differences.

entries.misconception: We add –s to make irregular plurals.
entries.identify: Ask learners: Can we say: Peoples like to go to parks. Childrens like waterslides. If necessary, clarify that the answer is no, because people and children are irregular plurals. This means we have to remember that they are different.
entries.overcome: Make a working wall or hanging display of irregular plurals as a reminder for learners to use when speaking or writing.

entries.misconception: You have to start all over again if you have forgotten to write something when sharing news.
entries.identify: Ask the class if they write letters. Ask what happens if they have finished and then remember something important that they wanted to write. Take learners’ ideas. Tell them about the term ’P.S.’ (postscript, which means after writing), which allows you to add something to a note, postcard or letter after it has been written.
entries.overcome: Remind learners of other ways to add information in non-fiction writing: • P.S. in a note, letter or postcard • text in a Tip box • text in a Did you know? / Fact

entries.misconception: All learners find it easy to hear rhyme.
entries.identify: Say a word, e.g. me Ask learners to say a rhyming word. Note who finds this easy and who struggles. Play rhyming snap. Hand out word cards to learners that feature words that rhyme but are decodable. Ask learners to find their rhyming partners. Ask them why they are standing together to elicit the discussion about rhyme.
entries.overcome: Use the Phonics Workbook A, pages 4–5.

entries.misconception: to is always spelled with letter t and o.
entries.identify: Ask learners (or selected learners if coming to write on the board) to write down three short dictated sentences: I go to the shops. I have two hens. I have a cat, too. Check each sentence and talk about the different spellings of this word.
entries.overcome: Agree a class code so that each time the word is misspelled, you can say the ‘secret code’ to alert learners to check the spelling of the word, e.g. two clicks of the fingers or say Toucan!

entries.misconception: We can only use the verb to say when finishing direct speech.
entries.identify: Ask learners to read the sentence: ‘Fire! Fire!’ says Obadiah. Ask: Could we change the word ‘says’? What verb could we use instead of say.
entries.overcome: Make a class working wall or hanging display of words to replace says/said. When writing, encourage learners to use the wall or display as a word bank.

entries.misconception: Red is one colour and one word. With learners, make a collection of ‘red’ things from around the classroom.
entries.identify: Ask: If they are all red, why do they look different? Do we know different words that mean ‘red’ or ‘a type of red’? entries.misconception: We do not need to notice full stops when reading.

entries.overcome: Remind learners they need to take a tiny pause at the full stop when reading aloud. Provide plenty of read-aloud modelling as well as opportunities for learners to practise. Remind learners to notice the full stops as they read.

entries.misconception: Verbs ending in –ed all sound like /d/
entries.identify: Ask learners to read the verb gobbled, which ends with a /d/ sound. Repeat with the word shocked. Learners may say the word ending in /g/, but explain that there are two digraphs (sh, ck) and that the –ed ending is spelled ed but pronounced /t/.
entries.overcome: Remind learners of the different ways to pronounce ed when they encounter them in their reading. Play games to sort verbs ending in –ed by sound. You may also wish to introduce the /id/ pronunciation, too, e.g. sorted.

entries.misconception: Traditional stories always begin with Once upon a time and end with And they all lived happily ever after. Note what beginnings and endings learners are using in their own stories – either written or verbal.
entries.raw: Traditional stories always begin / with Once upon a time and end / with And they all lived happily / ever after. / Note what beginnings and endings / learners are using in their own / stories – either written or verbal. / Ask learners to try to recall some / of the ways traditional tales begin / and end. / Explore the language together: / Long, long ago / One fine day. / Back in time when animals could / talk … / In a land far, far away / And that was the end of the … / And that is how the story ends. / And from that day to this … / And the x was never seen again.

entries.misconception: Traditional stories are always about characters joining each other one by one on a journey.
entries.raw: Traditional stories are always about / characters joining each other one / by one on a journey. / Ask learners if all traditional stories / are about adding characters one by / one. / Share other traditional stories that / do not involve adding characters / on a journey.

entries.misconception: We always have to use the correct name for things in our writing.
entries.identify: Ask learners to listen to the opening of the story: One day in the leaves of the eucalyptus tree hung a scare in the air where no eye could see, … What do they think the ‘scare in the air’ is? (It’s the snake.)
entries.overcome: Create a class resource of fun phrases like this: A fright in the night (a night creature) An eye in the sky (a bird)

entries.misconception: Listening for rhyme does not help our reading and spelling.
entries.identify: Ask learners to read with you and fill in a simple cloze written on the board. ‘Do you think,’ said the snake to the boy with the ________, ‘that there’s room for something yummy with you inside my _______?’ Show how boy/toy and yummy/tummy share spelling patterns.
entries.overcome: Practise phonic games and provide further simple dictations where learners must use one spelling pattern to write another word. Note that the spelling patterns will not always be the same for rhyming words, e.g. The snake had a tummy ache!

entries.misconception: Clapping syllables is the same as clapping phonemes / letter sounds.
entries.identify: Ask learners to clap the word skipped. Repeat these games frequently. Ask learners to use this strategy in their writing work to help them work out how many and which letters to use.
entries.overcome: Use the Starter idea.

entries.misconception: We can use phonics to decode all words.
entries.identify: Ask learners to read these words: can, toy, slurp, the, said. Ask how they worked out how to read these words. They probably used phonics for /c/ /a/ /n/, /t/ /oy/, /s/ /l/ /ur/ /p/, but may have found it difficult for the and said.
entries.overcome: Talk about high-frequency or tricky words, and how sometimes we have to use phonics as our first approach and then try other ways to work out a word if phonics cannot help us get all the way there. Encourage learners to use phonics first and then, if necessary, use other strategies to work out a word. Explain that for high-frequency words, we sometimes just have to learn to recognise them, e.g. the, said.

entries.misconception: We always have to say every letter sound in a word.
entries.identify: Write the word sign on the board. Ask learners to say the sounds and blend them to read the word. They may say: /s/ /i/ /g/ /n/ and wonder how the letter sounds help us to read the word.
entries.overcome: Explain to learners that we always start by using phonics to sound out words, but sometimes we have to try out other letter sound possibilities to sound the word correctly. Model saying /s//igh/ /n/ and talk through how to try using a long /igh/ rather than a short /i/ and then how to jump over the silent g. Find different examples of words with tricky letters or unstressed vowels but linked to the topic, e.g. labels (unstressed e); ice (c as /s/ ). Remind learners, when they are struggling with a word, that they might need to try other letter sound

entries.misconception: Capital letters are just bigger versions of lower-case letters.
entries.identify: Ask learners to look at a sign written in lower-case letters and one written in capitals. Ask: What do you notice?
entries.overcome: Highlight letters that are the same: s and S, w and W, p and P What do they notice about other letters, such as: b and B, h and H? Provide a class frieze for learners to use when they are unsure how to write a letter in either case. Allow peer-assessment time: Encourage learners to choose a word from their writing and talk about it with a partner. They should check for correct letter size, comparative sizing and correct use of lower-case and capital letters.

entries.misconception: Seeing –le at the end of a word means we say luh.
entries.identify: Write some words ending in –le on the board, e.g. purple, bottle, juggle, giggle. Ask learners to read them.
entries.overcome: Model how to sound them out to demonstrate that –le is two letters but one sound /l/. Create a –le word bank for learners to use when writing. Remind learners how to respond to words ending in –le when reading.

entries.misconception: Listening to a series of instructions is difficult. •
entries.raw: Listening to a series of instructions / is difficult. / • / Ask learners to follow a series / of simple instructions, e.g. / stand up, sit down, put your / arms on your head and close / your eyes. / • / Ask them what they are doing / to understand and follow your / instructions. / • / Ask: What makes listening / difficult? entries.misconception: There is only one type of book.
entries.raw: There is only one type of book. / Ask learners in small groups to talk / about books you provide for them, / e.g. a story book, a poetry book, an / annual, stories and recipes. / Ask what sort of books they have. / Invite learners to find other books / that include more than one type of / content, e.g. anthologies, poems / and puzzles. / Show learners that books are / varied and exciting. When they go / to a library to choose a book, they / should remember this.

entries.misconception: Two words cannot make one word with a different meaning.
entries.raw: Two words cannot make one word / with a different meaning. / Ask learners to read these words: / Lady / Bird / ladybird / Ask: How are the meanings / different? / List other compound words / together, e.g. windmill, keyboard, / sunflower, butterfly.

entries.misconception: Finding small words within words is just a fun thing to do.
entries.identify: Ask learners to read these words and find other words in them: Square/are (Knowing are does not help us read square.) Penguin/pen/in (Knowing pen and in helps us to read penguin.)
entries.overcome: Remind learners to try this technique when they are trying to work out an unknown word using their phonics. Sometimes it may be helpful.

entries.misconception: We can only use numbers to show the correct order of instructions.
entries.identify: Ask learners to recall what they have learned about how to show the correct order of instructions. They will probably say: We use numbers. Ask learners if there is another way to show order, e.g. arrows connecting boxes, showing something in a flow chart or as a circle, adding letters a, b, c, etc.
entries.overcome: Remind learners to always think about the best features to use when showing the correct order of instructions.

entries.misconception: We can call all instructions recipes. Show learners a recipe and ask them what it is called.
entries.identify: Show them different instructions from the unit and ask them whether we can call them recipes.
entries.overcome: Establish that the word recipe only applies to cooking instructions. Reinforce the meaning of the word recipe.

entries.misconception: Instructions sound rude and bossy.
entries.identify: Ask learners to tell you how to do something. They may sit: Sit down! or Drink your cup of tea! or similar. Ask them to ask you again, this time politely.
entries.overcome: Talk about how adding please can sound more polite when we are talking to someone we know. Check that this is true in our texts in the unit. Check with learners, when they are saying or writing instructions, whether they feel they should add please or not. It will help them to consider audience and purpose.

entries.misconception: We join from capital letters.
entries.identify: Ask one or all learners to copy and join a sentence from the rhyme in this session beginning with My …. Check they are beginning with a capital letter and ending with a full stop. Check they are not joining from the capital M.
entries.overcome: Use the Workbook Session 6.1 activities for joining practice. Create a class dangle to hang from a washing line: WE NEVER JOIN TO OR FROM CAPITAL LETTERS.

entries.misconception: The alphabet is just a sequence of letters that we have to learn how to say.
entries.identify: Ask learners to say the alphabet together as a class. Then ask if anyone can sing the alphabet in a song. Then ask: What else can we do with the alphabet? What else does it help us to do?
entries.overcome: Make a class A–Z of feelings. Continue to add words to each letter flag as you work through this unit. Learners will realise that the alphabet is helpful for creating fun displays that can then help them with their reading and writing.

entries.misconception: When we add –s, -ed or –ing, there is no change to the spelling of the root verb.
entries.identify: Ask learners to look at sets of verbs you write on the board: laugh, cheer (no change with verb endings) smile, dance (drop e with verb endings) grin, chat (double consonant with verb endings) Ask them to work quickly in pairs or groups to add the verb endings to each. Ask: What do you notice?
entries.overcome: Discuss with learners how they might remember to check their spellings when adding the verb endings. You could create a class poster for learners to use as they write.

entries.misconception: We always have to pronounce every letter in a word.
entries.identify: Write the word Wednesday on the board. Say it in two ways and ask learners which is correct: Wed-nes-day Wensday
entries.overcome: Use this as an example. Then select other words that feature silent letters or unstressed syllables, e.g. surprise, pronounced su’prise. Encourage learners to play ‘I say, you say’-type games in which they must repeat correct pronunciation, or games that ask them to select the correct pronunciation. Reading aloud will also help with this.

entries.misconception: Lists are just for reminding us of things to do or what to buy at the shops.
entries.identify: Ask half the class to talk with partners about the places the dragons visit. Ask the other half of the class to talk about how the dragons fly in the story. As they provide answers, write them in a list.
entries.overcome: Talk about how writing lists can help us to make notes or to remember things.

entries.misconception: Illustrations are of things that are not real and photos are of things that are real.
entries.identify: Show learners an illustration of something real, e.g. an apple, and a photo of something pretend, e.g. a boy flying. Ask: Which is real and which is pretend? Find different examples of illustrations and photos to explore their use.
entries.overcome: Use Learner’s Book Session 7.2 Activity 3.

entries.misconception: Full stops do not tell us what to do. Ask learners to read a small extract: The boy thought he would never catch a star. Just then he noticed something floating in the water. It was the prettiest star he had ever seen. Just a baby star.
entries.identify: Ask them how many full stops they can see (four). Ask them what full stops are for. (They might tell you that they show the end of sentence / they tell you to pause/breathe.) Draw learners’ attention to the other full stops in the full text.
entries.overcome: Remind learners what full stops tell us in their one-to-one reading aloud sessions.

entries.misconception: We only answer questions with yes or no.
entries.identify: Ask learners a series of closed questions: Do/Did you …?; Can/could you …?; Are/Were you …? What do they notice about their responses, (They are all yes or no.) Then ask them a few open questions, using question words: why, how, what, etc. Now what do they notice about their responses? (They do not feature yes or no.)
entries.overcome: Help learners to be aware of their questions and their responses in talk sessions. Remind them as opportunities arise. You may wish to use the terms open and closed questions if appropriate for your class.

entries.misconception: We can only use one adjective to describe something.
entries.identify: Look at the photos in Learner’s Book Session 7.6 Getting started. Ask learners to describe each photo. If they respond with just one adjective, e.g. tall grass, ask: How else can we describe the grass? e.g. Feathery, long, tall grass …
entries.overcome: Remind learners that in their speech and writing they can use two or three adjectives to describe something to make it more accurate and interesting, e.g. a big, dark forest or a big, deep, dark forest. (See Plenary activity.) If appropriate for your learners draw their attention to the use of the comma.

entries.misconception: Letter q has the sound /kyoo/
entries.identify: Ask learners to tell you the letter name for Qq (letter Q). Ask them for its letter sound.
entries.overcome: Explain that it has no sound on its own – it must have the letter u with it: qu makes the sound /kwu/ as in queen or quiz. Ask learners to read some words that feature qu, e.g. squeeze, squelch, squish. Remind learners when they are reading aloud or spelling that if there is a q there will also be a u and we say /kwu/. Also mention that many words begin with squ ….

entries.misconception: Words in a sentence can be in any order.
entries.identify: Ask learners to read a jumbled sentence. Ask them if it makes sense and to say why. Ask them to sort the words into the correct order. Ask: How do they know what order to put the words in?
entries.overcome: Remind learners that a sentence must make sense when you read it back. If it does not, then you have to re-order the words. Explain that we can use the capital letter and a full stop as clues in this type of activity.

entries.identify: Ask learners to look at a book in small groups. Ask: What does the front cover tell you? What does the back cover tell you?
entries.overcome: Talk about using all the information on a book cover to gauge what the book is about and whether learners want to read it.

entries.misconception: Questions always begin with a question word.
entries.identify: Ask learners to ask questions about an animal. Do they only use question words? e.g. What?, Why?, When? Can they ask a question that does not begin with a question word? e.g. Is it a mammal? Does it swim fast?

entries.misconception: Desert and dessert are pronounced the same and mean the same.

entries.overcome: Model how to say both words with the stress falling either at the beginning or the end of the word: desert: des-ert dessert: dess-ert Model the use of each word in a sentence: What is for dessert today? Did you choose the desert as your topic?

entries.misconception: If there are words with zz then you must be able to write words with xx and yy.

entries.overcome: Remind learners that many consonants can appear in words as double letters, but not x or y (and not hh, jj, kk, qq or ww). Consider making a class poster to summarise this learning message for reference during writing work.

entries.misconception: What someone thinks is always a fact.
entries.identify: Tell learners that you think baby penguins love the sunshine. Ask them if what you have said is a fact. Is it true? Or is it what you think?
entries.overcome: Discuss the differences between something that is a fact (true) and something that is an opinion (someone’s own view, which may not be true). Encourage learners to question what they read in information books. Ask: How do we know something is a fact? Some books give lots of information to help us believe the facts. Tell learners to ask themselves: How can we check?

entries.identify: Ask learners to tell you the difference between a fact file and a report.
entries.overcome: Explain that both provide facts, but a fact file is more likely to have lists of facts and a report more likely to have sentences with facts in them. Try to incorporate fact files and reports into other areas of learning to consolidate experience.

entries.misconception: We always read and write English left to right and top to bottom.
entries.identify: Ask learners how they read and write their first language. Ask: Do you read and write to the right or across the left? Do you read and write top to bottom or bottom to top? Ask them how we read and write English. (left to right, top to bottom) Ask them for examples of when we might see English written in different ways.
entries.overcome: Make a class display of texts in English that are written in different directions, e.g. acrostic poems, calligrams, jokes, crossword puzzles, text on fun birthday cards, text in some advertisements, text in some picture books (e.g. you could research online the books of Dr. Seuss or Lauren Child).

entries.misconception: We usually use colour and size to describe something.
entries.identify: Ask learners to describe the sun. They may say: big, round, yellow, hot, etc. Then ask if anyone can describe the sun, asking: Can you say how hot it is? How round it is? How yellow it is? Then explain that in asking these questions, you are already describing the sun!
entries.overcome: Create a checklist for describing things: • Think about size, colour, position, shape. • Use your senses. • Ask questions: How …? Isn’t it funny how … • Make statements: I do not

entries.misconception: We only add –s or –es for plural nouns, e.g. cloud – clouds, fox – foxes.
entries.identify: Ask learners to look at sets of verbs and nouns on the board: Verbs Nouns to kiss a kiss to dance a dance to flash a flash Ask them to say the verbs in the third person (he, she, it) and the nouns as plurals. Ask: What do you notice?
entries.overcome: Discuss with learners how they might remember to check their spellings when writing in the third person and when making nouns plural. You could create a class poster with them to use as they write.

entries.misconception: We compare things to show how different they are.
entries.identify: Ask learners to compare Jackie and Zuleika. Notice if they only say how they are different or whether they mention things that are also the same. Ask learners to compare other things, e.g. the weather yesterday and today. If you made a weather chart, use it to compare weather on different days.
entries.overcome: Emphasise how comparing things can show us both differences and similarities.

entries.identify: Ask learners to describe one of the characters. They may well use adjectives. entries.overcome: Discuss the answers and show how thinking and talking can help you to make a prediction with reason. Even if it’s not correct it shows a good thinking process.

entries.misconception: The following words are not verbs: is, was, am, can, think.
entries.identify: When asking learners to ‘act out’ single words (e.g. eat, sleep, mouse, laugh, chair) learners can confuse the nouns and verbs. For example: in ‘be a mouse’ they might think the word ‘mouse’ can be demonstrated and therefore is the verb. Ask learners: Are you mousing or are you being a mouse? Point out that the verb in that sentence is being.
entries.overcome: Suggest learners use the following test to identify verbs: if the words can follow I or he then it may be a verb (e.g. I know; I think; I can; I am; he is). If the word can follow the then it is not a verb (e.g. the child; the crocodile).

entries.misconception: Mail means email.

entries.misconception: Scanning a text means reading every word in a text very quickly.
entries.identify: Observe learners carefully as they scan a text. Learners who move their heads rapidly are often simply moving over a text without reading anything.
entries.overcome: Explain that scanning a text involves thinking about the text before reading it so that learners can make a sensible decision about where particular information may be in a text. Ask: Where in a letter will you find information about where someone lives (e.g. in the address)? Where will you find the address (e.g. at the top of the letter)? Where you find the name of the letter writer (e.g. at the end of a letter)? Explain that thinking like this helps you move to the correct place in a text quickly to find an answer.

entries.misconception: Good morning and Greetings are formal greetings.
entries.identify: Ask learners to fill out a table of informal and formal greetings. Some learners may insert Good morning and Greetings in the formal column in the table.
entries.overcome: Explain that these are both informal greetings that are sometimes used in formal writing, especially in emails. entries.misconception: Multi-clause sentences are all conditional sentences.
entries.identify: Ask learners to complete Activity 3. Some learners may add extra information to the main clause and not a condition. Write the following sentence on the board: You can go out to play and run around.
entries.overcome: Explain to learners the actions are not connected. Now write: You can go out to play if you want to run around. Explain that learners will only be allowed to run around if they go outside. Running around is a condition of the second part of the sentence.

entries.misconception: Learners identify like / love / enjoy statements as facts. Note learners‘ answers when asked to identify fact and opinion statements in the Getting started activity.

entries.misconception: Rhyming words in poems give a poem its rhythm.
entries.identify: Ask learners to read Kite aloud. Note learners who read the poem as if it is a rhyming poem (e.g. pausing at the words flight and height) to give the poem a rhythm.
entries.overcome: Explain that not all poems have rhyming words and that rhyming words can sometimes be within a line, rather than at the end. Ask: Why do poets start new lines (e.g. to give the poem a shape, to show us the rhythm)? Explain that the shape of the poem and the way the lines are written are more important than rhyming words and that this is what gives a poem its rhythm.

entries.misconception: The start of a fiction story is usually the same, like once upon a time or long, long ago.
